The U.S. wages and employment on this page come from BLS OEWS 2025 data and BLS employment projections 2024—2034 as presented by O*NET; the precise occupational wage for mainland China was not obtained and is registered as a visible gap; the two jurisdictions and their work systems must not be applied to one another.

To judge whether home appliance repair suits you, first run one verifiable troubleshooting drill using public or simulated materials: choose a fictional appliance (for example, a washer that will not drain), and write a step-by-step process from taking the call and questioning the customer, confirming the fault symptoms, consulting schematics and manuals, cutting power and water and doing a safety check, testing section by section with instruments, locating and replacing the part, to reassembling, test running, explaining to the customer, and billing and collecting payment, marking the safety check points and possible abnormalities at each step (live working, gas leaks, mismatched parts, customer information and cost disputes). Afterward, check: whether cutting power and gas and confirming safety are treated as non-omittable items; whether situations beyond your individual authority, such as gas and live working, are written as stop-and-escalate; and whether you have marked the basis for repair versus replacement decisions and how costs are described. Test with a real deliverable, not just answers to an interest questionnaire.

Fit signals | The work activity importance ratings for U.S. O*NET 49-9031.00 show that operating vehicles, mechanized devices, or equipment (78), getting information (77), performing for or working directly with the public (77), updating and using relevant knowledge (77), handling and moving objects (76), and making decisions and solving problems (75) are the most important activities for this occupation; work context shows that telephone conversations 97% report every day, face-to-face discussions 89% report every day, contact with others 87%, using hands to handle or feel objects and tools 78% report continually or almost continually, in an enclosed vehicle or equipment 78% report every day, dealing with external customers or the public 77% report extremely important, frequency of decision making 77% report every day, freedom to make decisions 70% report a lot of freedom, indoors, environmentally controlled 59% report every day, and work week 49% report 40 hours. The most important skills are critical thinking, speaking, active listening, and reading comprehension. If you are willing to do hands-on repair on site or in a workshop, explain problems directly to customers, and judge to procedure within electrical and gas safety boundaries, these daily demands are closer to the way you work.

Caution signals | O*NET also shows (49-9031.00): dealing with external customers or the public 77% report extremely important, telephone conversations 97% report every day, contact with others 87%, freedom to make decisions 70% report a lot of freedom, frequency of decision making 77% report every day, exposure to contaminants 45% report every day, exposure to minor burns, cuts, bites, or stings 35% report every day, and cramped work space or awkward positions 53% report once a week or more. This occupation deals with customers' appliances, live electrical and gas components, and on-site service settings: a single misjudged live-working decision, a single mishandled gas leak, or a single misdiagnosis can cause personal injury or customer property loss and cost disputes. This page therefore lists cutting power and gas and safety confirmation, the basis for fault judgments, costs and customer communication, and authorization boundaries separately. On the U.S. side, this occupation itself is not marked Bright Outlook, and the O*NET summary shows projected growth at the average level (3%—4%) from 2024 to 2034, with about 3,100 job openings per year, from employment of about 37,300 in 2024. If it is hard for you to sustain direct customer communication, travel to service calls, or live electrical and gas risk, you should treat these as real costs that need careful weighing.

Commitment judgment | Real fit comes from whether you can do three things on the same repair job at once: make the repair solid (complete disassembly, troubleshooting, replacement, reassembly, and test running based on fault symptoms and manuals, producing reviewable repair and inspection records); keep safety and compliance boundaries under control (cutting power and gas, handling and escalating gas and live working, and communicating about customer information and costs per institutional and regulatory requirements, without overstepping to handle work beyond your authority); and carry definable position responsibility (be responsible for your own repair judgments and records, while referring work beyond your individual authorization to qualified personnel under institutional rules). It is recommended to test this with one verifiable experience (completing a step-by-step troubleshooting process and inspection record, or a drill on identifying and handling common faults), rather than relying only on the conclusions of an interest questionnaire.

The daily work of home appliance repairers can be broken down along three lines: (1) taking calls and diagnosis—communicating with customers to determine faults, consulting schematics and manuals, and using test tools to locate problems; (2) repair and installation—disassembling, replacing parts, reassembling and test running, installing and leveling appliances, and connecting water or gas lines; (3) customers and records—explaining repair or replacement recommendations and costs, billing and collecting payment, and recording what was done. The three lines share the same set of safety and judgment requirements, but their deliverables go to different recipients: diagnosis and repair are delivered to the customer's appliance, while customers and records serve the customer relationship and service ledger.

subject.name: Home Appliance Repairers
subject.summary: Home Appliance Repairers corresponds to the precise U.S. O*NET/SOC 49-9031.00 occupation "Home Appliance Repairers": repairing, adjusting, or installing all types of electric or gas household appliances, such as refrigerators, washers, dryers, and ovens. Official scope text: Repair, adjust, or install all types of electric or gas household appliances, such as refrigerators, washers, dryers, and ovens. Core tasks include billing customers for repair work and collecting payment (importance 87), observing and inspecting appliances while running (86), talking with customers or reviewing work orders to determine faults (86), referring to schematics and manuals (85), and tracing and testing circuits to locate shorts and grounds (85). The U.S. wages and employment on this page come from BLS OEWS 2025 and BLS employment projections 2024—2034 as presented by O*NET (the precise occupation 49-9031.00); the precise occupational wage for mainland China was not obtained and is registered as a visible gap; China's work safety and product quality institutional boundaries are labeled separately.
